Josephus text: Gutenberg #2848, translator William Whiston (1737; Whiston died 1752), file header checked. Extract is Antiquities 18.3.2–3 and 20.9.1 verbatim, footnote markers stripped, Whiston's own square-bracket insertions ([the], [or, some of his companions], [Agrippa], [to exercise his authority]) kept. About 720 words.

Josephus interpolation: the majority view (partial authenticity: a neutral core of 18.3.3 with Christian additions such as 'if it be lawful to call him a man', 'He was [the] Christ', 'he appeared to them alive again the third day') and the near-consensus authenticity of 20.9.1 are standard (see e.g. J. P. Meier, A Marginal Jew vol. 1, 1991, ch. 3; the 10th-century Arabic version of Agapius, published by Shlomo Pines, 1971). A minority, e.g. Richard Carrier, argue 'who was called Christ' in 20.9.1 is also an interpolation. Josephus's Antiquities dated AD 93–94 (Ant. 20.267: thirteenth year of Domitian). Reviewer: confirm wording 'most scholars' / 'widely accepted'.

Pliny text: Gutenberg #2811, 'Letters of Pliny', translator William Melmoth (died 1799; translation 1746), revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet (Bohn's Classical Library, 1878). I could not confirm Bosanquet's death date; the revision was published long before 1929. In this edition the letters are numbered X.XCVII and X.XCVIII; standard numbering is Letters 10.96 and 10.97. Two obvious transcription slips in the Gutenberg file were corrected: "officiate'" -> "officiate" and "Secundtis" -> "Secundus" (Trajan's reply). Reviewer may prefer to restore the file text exactly. The letter's main paragraph is long (about 770 words) because the source has it as one paragraph; not split.

Pliny claims: governor of Bithynia-Pontus about AD 110–113; letter usually dated about AD 112; 'two female slaves ... said to officiate' translates Latin 'ministrae' (often rendered deaconesses). 'A form of prayer to Christ, as to a divinity' renders 'carmen Christo quasi deo', often translated 'a hymn to Christ as to a god'. Pliny's dates (about 61 – about 113) are approximate. 'About eighty years after the cross' assumes crucifixion about AD 30 and letter about 112.

Mark is the earliest Gospel: majority scholarly view (Markan priority), stated as 'most scholars think'. Gospel dating 'roughly forty to seventy years after Jesus' assumes Mark about AD 70 and John about 90–100; some scholars date Mark earlier.

1 Corinthians written about AD 53–55 (from Ephesus, 1 Cor 16:8). The early dating of the formula in 15:3–8 (often to within a few years of the crucifixion) is widely held, including by sceptical scholars; e.g. Gerd Lüdemann and Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) treat it as pre-Pauline tradition. Reviewer: check Ehrman's precise dating if 'sceptical ones included' is kept.
'At a time when a woman's testimony carried little weight' (S6): commonly argued from Josephus Ant. 4.8.15 and rabbinic sources; some scholars think the point is overstated. Consider softening.
Crucifixion as punishment for slaves and rebels, meant to shame: standard (Martin Hengel, Crucifixion, 1977).

Boethius biography: born about 477, executed 524 (some sources 524/525); consul 510, magister officiorum under Theodoric; imprisoned traditionally at Pavia (ancient Ticinum). Place of imprisonment is the tradition, not certain: some sources place his execution in the 'ager Calventianus' near Milan. 'One of the most read books of the Middle Ages' is the standard judgement (e.g. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Boethius').
Boethius as Christian who does not invoke Christ or Scripture in the Consolation: standard scholarly observation (SEP 'Boethius'); he also wrote theological tractates on the Trinity.

Leonard lived 1876–1944, so the text meets the public-domain rule; the brief suggested Munro but Munro is not on GITenberg as far as I could find. Verse lines are kept with '\n' line breaks inside each paragraph: the reader view may need white-space: pre-line to show them.

Lucretius line references (Latin numbering III.830–869, 894–930, 970–977) are my mapping of Leonard's passages to the Latin ('nil igitur mors est ad nos' 830; 'iam iam non domus accipiet te laeta' 894; 'frigida vitai pausa' 930; 'vitaque mancipio nulli datur, omnibus usu' 971; 'respice item' 972). Please check. Two cuts marked '…': the passage on imagining one's own corpse (870–893) and the section 931–969, partly cut because Nature's speech there asks 'why not rather make an end of life', which I judged unsuitable for a pastoral reading.

Lucretius dates about 99–55 BC and 'Rome, about 55 BC' are approximate (the poem is thought to have circulated around 54 BC; Cicero mentions it in a letter of February 54 BC, Ad Quintum fratrem II.9).
Epicurus 'death is nothing to us': Letter to Menoeceus 124–125 and Principal Doctrines 2.

Bunyan, The Pilgrim's Progress, Part One, from Gutenberg #131 (GITenberg repo name The-Pilgrim-s-Progress-from-this-world-to-that-which-is-to-come--13-Delivered-under-the-similit__131, found in gitberg's GITenberg_repo_list.tsv). Paragraph numbers {389}–{394} and {400}–{402}, with one cut marked '…'. I removed the edition's paragraph numbers, bracketed scripture references, a marginal note ('In the Resurrection of the Righteous') and a marginal heading ('Christian's conflict at the hour of death').

Bunyan facts: born 1628, died 1688; tinker by trade; imprisoned 1660–1672 for preaching without a licence; Part One first published in London in 1678. 'Wrote much of his book while imprisoned' is the common account (he says in the book he wrote it in a 'den'); some date the writing to a later, shorter imprisonment of 1675–76. 'Baptist preacher': he led the independent Bedford congregation, usually described as Baptist. Please check wording.
Gerontius: Newman's poem 1865, Elgar 1900; 'This is the best of me' from music.json (Elgar inscribed it on the score, quoting Ruskin).
Brahms Requiem: second movement sets 1 Peter 1:24 ('Denn alles Fleisch, es ist wie Gras'); the track in music.json is the fourth movement 'Wie lieblich sind deine Wohnungen' (Psalm 84).

Handel's Messiah: the Hallelujah chorus ends Part Two; Part Three sets 1 Corinthians 15:51–57 ('Behold, I tell you a mystery', 'The trumpet shall sound', 'O death, where is thy sting'). The music.json track is the Hallelujah chorus.

Chardin's Soap Bubbles: the soap bubble as an image of life's brevity (homo bulla) is a standard reading of the motif; I phrase it as what painters of the time 'often' meant, not as Chardin's stated intention.
All painting descriptions use only the title, artist and alt text in art.json; several alt texts are truncated, so I kept to their first sentences.

Library depths used: awe-and-wonder 2 (What Christians believe: 'the fear of the Lord'), athens-and-jerusalem 1, are-we-more-than-machines 4, suffering 1, who-was-jesus 4, what-happens-when-we-die 2. awe-and-wonder is used because Ecclesiastes 3:11 and 3:14 speak of eternity set in the heart and fear before God; drop it if a reviewer feels it is a stretch.

New conversation wright-bird-afterlife-ndes: title, date (23 Mar 2025), hosts and description verified on the official Premier page https://www.premier.plus/ask-nt-wright-anything/podcasts/episodes/what-happens-when-we-die-nt-wright-on-the-afterlife-and-ndes (WebFetch). The summary uses only that public description. The insight's claim about Surprised by Hope (2008) is from the book and the existing Library entry, not from the episode; I phrased it as 'listen for whether'. A Christian Post article (13 Aug 2026) reports Wright urging caution on NDEs on the same podcast, possibly a later episode (premierunbelievable.com article 21995), so I did not use its quotes.
Bart Ehrman and Rowan Williams–Richard Dawkins: existing entries harris-ehrman-christianity and williams-dawkins, used unchanged.
Closing: All Saints' Day 1 November; All Souls' Day 2 November, kept especially by Catholics and Anglicans (and some Lutherans).
Pastoral: session 4 practice points to real help (a friend, a minister or a bereavement service). The journey deals with grief and should have a pastor's read before review.

No research papers: there is no peer-reviewed science that bears directly on what happens after death, and near-death-experience studies are treated through the Wright conversation rather than as evidence.
how-we-got-here: Thucydides reading: Crawley translation (1874; Crawley died 1893), Gutenberg 7142 via GITenberg. The Gutenberg text has no section numbers; I mapped the paragraphs to II.37, II.38, II.40, II.41 (first sentence only) and II.45 from the standard division. Please check against a numbered edition. II.39 and II.42–44 are cut and marked '…'. Each paragraph in the source opens with an unclosed speech quotation mark (the convention for a continuing speech); I removed that leading mark, and changed nothing else.

The Funeral Oration was delivered in the winter of 431/430 BC; Thucydides' dates (about 460 to about 400 BC) are approximate; he says he served as a general (IV.104–105). 'Written after 431 BC' is deliberately vague because the date of composition is uncertain.
The learn lines whole-earth-their-tomb come from II.43, which the reading leaves out, so they are not repeated.

Augustine reading: City of God XXII.24, from Gutenberg 45305 (T. & T. Clark, Edinburgh, 1871). The volume's title page says Marcus Dods translated it, except Books IV, XVII and XVIII (George Wilson) and V–VIII (J. J. Smith), so Book XXII is Dods's (he died 1909). Gutenberg's header calls him 'Editor: Marcus Dodds' (sic). Footnote markers stripped, '--' turned into em dashes. The reading is the chapter's third paragraph, then the fifth, cut after the quotation of Romans 8:32; the cuts are marked '…'. City of God was finished about 426 (traditional dating); Augustine lived 354–430.

Douglass reading: the Appendix to the Narrative (Boston: Anti-Slavery Office, 1845), Gutenberg 23 via GITenberg (Narrative-of-the-Life-of-Frederick-Douglass-an-American-Slave_23). Original English, so no translator. Paragraph 1, then (after the cut of Whittier's verses and the Matthew 23 quotation) the 'Dark and terrible' and 'Such is, very briefly' paragraphs. Italic underscores removed. The first paragraph includes his line about a sister sold 'for purposes of prostitution'; I kept it because it is verbatim and central, but a reviewer may want to consider it. Douglass's birth year (about 1818), escape (1838) and death (1895) should be checked against a standard biography. 'kind' is set to 'church' (shown as 'From the Christian tradition'), since Douglass writes as a Christian critic; a reviewer may prefer another label.

I could not use Equiano: the GITenberg mirror of Gutenberg 15399 could not be found under any name I tried, and gutenberg.org is blocked here. Douglass was chosen instead because the brief asks for the Church's own record on slavery, and he states the case from inside the faith.

Bible Gateway refused my fetch (rate limited), so I checked WEB verses against the eng-web USFX file in the seven1m/open-bibles GitHub repository: Exodus 3:7, 3:14, Galatians 3:28, 4:7, Philemon 1:8–21. That edition uses 'Yahweh'; no verse with the divine name is quoted in my text.

Philemon: the 'runaway slave' reading is traditional, not certain. Some scholars argue Onesimus was not a fugitive but was sent to Paul, or had gone to him as a mediator; a few (e.g. Allen Dwight Callahan, 1993) argue he was Philemon's brother, not a slave. My text says only that he 'has left his master' or 'had left him', which fits most readings.
Isaiah 40 is described as addressed 'to a people in exile'. That is the usual scholarly reading (chapters 40–55 address exiles in Babylon), though traditional authorship views differ.
Rembrandt, Philemon and Baucis (1658): the story is from Ovid, Metamorphoses VIII; the gods are Jupiter and Mercury. Only Mercury is named in the art.json alt text; 'two strangers' follows Ovid.
Bourdon, The Finding of Moses: the alt text names the procession, the diadem, the infant in a basket and the man by the river. I call the infant Moses because of the title.

El Greco, Saint Martin and the Beggar: the cloak story is from Sulpicius Severus, Life of Saint Martin 3 (Amiens). The alt text shows the cloth being handed down, not cut; my line says 'by the old story' for that reason.
Song for Athene (Tavener, 1993) was written in memory of Athene Hariades, a young family friend killed in a cycling accident. Please check before publishing; I say only 'a young woman named Athene'.
O Come, O Come, Emmanuel: 'ransom captive Israel' is in J. M. Neale's translation (1851).
Byrd's Mass for Four Voices (about 1592–93) was published for recusant Catholic worship, as the music.json note says.
Palestrina, Missa Papae Marcelli: the 'saved polyphony at Trent' story is a legend, and the text says so.

Were You There: first printed in 1899 (William Barton, Old Plantation Hymns). That it began among enslaved African Americans is the traditional view, not documented, and my wording ('from African American Christians, whose people knew slavery') avoids claiming more.
Evidence (session 5): keltner-2003 is a theoretical review (no data) and piff-2015 is 5 studies with modest lab effects, both rated 'moderate' in research.json. The 'why' says the evidence is modest.

Session 4 links Nietzsche (does-morality-need-god, depth 4) to Philemon. The idea that Nietzsche called Christian ethics a 'slave revolt in morality' (Beyond Good and Evil §195; Genealogy of Morals I.7) stands behind the 'why' line, but the line itself only paraphrases the Library entry.
Depth numbers follow build.mjs, which leaves out 'Why it matters for you' and 'Reading list': 1 short answer, 2 what Christians believe, 3 great teachers, 4 modern debate, 5 sources.

Session 6 'why' names crusades and persecutions in general terms only; the session's reading and Library depth deal with slavery. A reviewer might want a crusades source added to the slavery-and-abolition or human-dignity entry later.
Practices avoid wellness habits. Session 1's practice mentions writing to a councillor, which is UK-specific; adjust if needed.
